narration: Meet Hopper, a frog. Hopper wants to cross a river on eight stepping stones, numbered zero to seven. Each hop goes forward one stone, or two. Drawn as a graph, each [[stone]]stone is a vertex, and each [[hop]]hop is an arrow, a directed edge. [[q]]How many different ways can Hopper get from stone zero to stone seven?

Let us count backward, from the far bank. [[s7]]From stone seven, Hopper is done. That is one way: do nothing. [[s6]]From stone six, one way: hop one. [[s5]]From stone five, two ways: hop one, then one more, or hop two, straight to the bank.

[[rule]]See the pattern? The ways from a stone are the ways from the stone one ahead, plus the ways from the stone two ahead, because those are the only first hops. [[s4]]Stone four: two plus one is three. [[s3]]Stone three: three plus two is five.
Keep going. [[s2]]Eight. [[s1]]Thirteen. [[s0]]And from stone zero, twenty-one ways. [[rule0]]Every count used only the counts of the stones it can hop to.

In any graph, this is called counting paths. The graph must be a [[dag]]DAG: a directed acyclic graph, meaning arrows, and no cycles. To count the paths from {s|S} to {t|T}: [[base]]if {s|S} is {t|T}, there is one path, the empty one. [[rec]]Otherwise, add up the counts of {s|S}'s children. The children are the vertices that {s|S} points to.

Here is the graph from your class lab. Vertex {A} points to {B} and {C}. {B} and {C} both point to {D}. {D} points to {E}. How many paths from {A} to {E}? [[b]]From {B} to {E}: one. [[c]]From {C} to {E}: one. [[a]]So from {A}: two. [[p1]]One path goes {A}, {B}, {D}, {E}. [[p2]]The other goes {A}, {C}, {D}, {E}.

The code asks these questions in a different order. [[go]]To count from {A}, it asks {B}. {B} asks {D}. {D} asks {E}, and {E} answers one. {D} answers one. {B} answers one. Then {A} asks {C}, and {C} asks {D} all over again. {D} has to ask {E} all over again. [[again]]The same question, twice. Seven calls, for five vertices.
That repeat is harmless here. On a bigger map, it explodes. This is a hiking map: seven junctions, twelve one-way trails, all uphill. [[q]]How many different routes lead from Start to Summit?
Plain recursion asks each child, and each child asks its own children, with no memory. [[go]]Watch the calls pile up. Twenty-four calls, for a map with seven junctions.
Look at the repeats. [[meadow]]Meadow is asked five times. [[falls]]Falls is asked four times. Every time, the answer is one, recomputed from scratch.

The fix: write each answer down the first time, and look it up after. That is called memoization, and the table is a cache. [[tree]]Here is the same search with a cache. [[hit]]Whenever a junction was already answered, it is a cache hit: read the table, and stop there.

Here is the table filling in. [[c1]]Summit: one. [[c2]]Meadow: one. [[c3]]Falls: one. [[c4]]Creek: two. [[c5]]Ridge: two. [[c6]]Pine: five. [[c7]]Start: nine. Nine routes. Each junction was finished only after all of its children.

Count the work. [[v]]Each junction is computed once: seven. [[e]]Each trail is looked at once, when its starting junction is computed: twelve. [[calls]]So there are thirteen calls: one for the start, plus one per trail. [[big]]That is V plus E: linear time.
Now your code. [[import]]The first line: from functools import cache. [[tool]]Functools is a toolbox that comes with Python, and cache is one tool in it.
[[def]]Def {count_paths|count~paths} takes the graph, a start {s|S}, and a target {t|T}. [[ret]]The last line, return nested of {s|S}, starts the whole search from the start.

[[at]]The line above the inner def is at cache. The at sign means: wrap the function underneath. [[wrap]]The wrapped function keeps a table of answers. The first time it sees an input, it runs, and writes the answer down. [[again]]The next time it sees the same input, it skips the function, and returns what is written.

[[nested]]Nested is a function inside a function, so it can read [[gg]]graph and [[tt]]{t|T} from outside. A new nested is built every time {count_paths|count~paths} is called, so its table starts empty each time. That is why the table can be keyed by {s|S} alone, even though the answer depends on {t|T}: inside one call, {t|T} never changes. [[shadow]]The {s|S} in the parentheses is a fresh variable: this call's vertex.
[[base]]If {s|S} equals {t|T}, [[one]]return one. Arriving at the target is exactly one path, the empty path. The parentheses around the comparison are optional.

Now the densest line. Return sum of nested of child, for child in graph of {s|S}. Take it apart. [[g]]Graph of {s|S} is the list of children of {s|S}. At vertex {A} in the diamond, that is {B} and {C}.

[[for]]For child in graph of {s|S} means: go through that list, one child at a time. [[nc]]Nested of child is the count for that child. Together they produce one number for each child. Wrapped in parentheses like this, it is called a generator expression.

[[sum]]Sum adds those numbers up. [[nothing]]If {s|S} has no children, there is nothing to add, and the sum of nothing is zero. [[long]]Here is the same thing written longhand: a total that starts at zero, a loop, and a return.

Run it on the diamond. [[t1]]{A} asks {B}, {B} asks {D}, {D} asks {E}, and {E} returns one. [[t2]]{D} is stored. {B} is stored. [[t3]]Then {A} asks {C}, and {C} asks {D}. [[t4]]A cache hit: one, instantly. {C} is stored. [[t5]]And {A} adds one plus one: two.
Your third test asks for {E} to {A}. [[e]]Nested of {E}: {E} is not {A}, and {E} has no children, so the sum of nothing is zero. Zero paths.

One rule: no cycles. Suppose vertex {A} pointed to vertex {B}, {B} to {C}, and {C} back to {A}. [[go]]Then nested of {A} would call {B}, which calls {C}, which calls {A} again, forever. [[err]]Python gives up with a recursion error. That is why the graph must be acyclic. In the book's words, the dependency graph of a recurrence must have no cycles.

Now your last test: sixty stepping stones, hop one or two. The test builds the graph in one line. [[comp]]For i in range sixty, make a key i, with the list i plus one, i plus two. [[bar]]The vertical bar merges two dictionaries, here adding stones sixty and sixty-one, which have no hops.

How many ways? [[big]]Two trillion, five hundred four billion, seven hundred thirty million, seven hundred eighty-one thousand, nine hundred sixty-one. [[fib]]Those are Fibonacci numbers, like the ones from the dynamic programming reading: each count is the sum of the two ahead.
Plain recursion would make over eight trillion calls. At ten million calls a second, that is more than nine days. [[cache]]With the cache: one hundred twenty-one calls. A fraction of a millisecond.

This is memoization, and it is depth-first search in disguise. [[m1]]Each junction is a vertex. [[m2]]Each call that needs another is an edge. [[m3]]Storing an answer is marking. [[m4]]Computing the value happens after the children, at the post-visit. The book puts it in one line: memoized recursion is depth-first search of the dependency graph.

To recap. [[c1]]Paths from {s|S} to {t|T}: one if {s|S} is {t|T}, otherwise the sum over the children. [[c2]]Plain recursion repeats work. [[c3]]A cache answers each vertex once, so the time is V plus E. [[c4]]And the answers come out children first. Next video: the other half of your lab, topological order.
